title: Capacity pool containment handoff and runbook draft
summary: Working notes and tentative runbook for on-call containment and handoff during GPU capacity pool degradation caused by noisy tenants and an aggressive autoscaler configuration. Includes quick triage steps, PromQL checks we used, candidate mitigation commands, and proposed post-incident follow-ups.
impact: Customers on dedicated capacity experienced elevated p99 token latency (2x baseline) and sporadic OOM evictions on 3 pools across us-west1 for ~45 minutes. No data loss; some requests timed out and retries hit fallback model variants.
timeline:
2026-02-20 03:12 UTC - PG alert: pool-p99-latency > 1200ms
2026-02-20 03:15 UTC - Pager triggered, on-call ack
2026-02-20 03:20 UTC - Observed spike in per-GPU memory utilization on hosts h-usw1-gpu-0[4-6]
2026-02-20 03:28 UTC - First eviction of low-priority containers to reclaim memory; autoscaler attempted scale-down shortly after
2026-02-20 03:30 UTC - Applied temporary tenant throttles and migrated 2 large jobs off noisy_hosts
2026-02-20 03:58 UTC - Latency returned to baseline after isolation and scale adjustments
2026-02-20 04:10 UTC - Incident declared mitigated; handoff to oncall-sre for follow-up
root_causes:
(hypotheses, ordered by likelihood)
1) Noisy tenant triggered sustained KV-cache inflation and pinned large tensor allocations; continuous batching increased per-session KV size beyond typical.
2) Autoscaler scale-down window was configured too aggressively (minReadySeconds too short), causing churn during transient load variations; combined with burst eviction policy, this amplified instability.
3) A kernel-level memory fragmentation pattern on a small subset of hosts reduced usable GPU memory and made evictions more likely. Evidence for (3) is sparse but should be tracked.
mitigation_steps:
Immediate triage checklist we used in the incident: 
- Step 0: Own the pager, notify #sre-ops and product-incident channel. 
- Step 1: Run node-level memory check (nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.used,memory.total --format=csv -i <host>) across suspected hosts.
- Step 2: Query Prometheus for per-tenant token throughput and per-session KV cache size (PromQL examples below).
- Step 3: If memory saturation on specific hosts, cordon the host and drain non-critical containers (kubectl cordon; kubectl drain --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force).
- Step 4: Apply short-term throttles at ingress (per-tenant qps cap) for tenants driving KV explosion. Update rate-limit config via gateway rollout.
- Step 5: Temporarily increase pool capacity if available (scale up reserved nodes) or switch routing policy to fallback lower-memory model variants.
- Step 6: Suspend aggressive scale-down signals: set autoscaler.min_ready_seconds=300 and increase stabilizationWindow to avoid churn during mitigation.
- Step 7: Monitor p50/p95/p99 and eviction_rate for 20 minutes before turning off throttles.
Notes: prefer migration -> throttle -> scale-out order. Eviction is last resort.
commands_executed:
Commands and snippets used during the oncall: 
- Bulk GPU check: for h in h-usw1-gpu-04 h-usw1-gpu-05 h-usw1-gpu-06; do ssh $h "nvidia-smi --query-gpu=index,name,memory.used,memory.total --format=csv"; done
- Per-container memory: ssh h-usw1-gpu-05 "docker stats --no-stream --format 'table {{.Name}}	{{.MemUsage}}' | sort -k2 -h"
- Drain host: kubectl cordon $NODE && kubectl drain $NODE --ignore-daemonsets --delete-emptydir-data --force
- Throttle rollout: curl -X POST -H 'Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN' https://gateway.redwood-inference.internal/ratelimit/update -d '{"tenant":"tenant-alpha","qps":10}'
- Autoscaler tweak: kubectl -n infra patch hpa pool-gpu-hpa --type=json -p '[{"op":"replace","path":"/spec/behavior/scaleDown/stabilizationWindowSeconds","value":300}]'
monitoring_queries:
PromQL snippets we relied on: 
- Per-pool p99 latency: histogram_quantile(0.99, sum(rate(pool_request_duration_seconds_bucket{pool=~"usw1-pool-.*"}[5m])) by (le,pool))
- Per-host GPU memory used: sum by (instance) (nv_gpu_memory_used_bytes) / sum by (instance) (nv_gpu_memory_total_bytes)
- Per-tenant KV cache size (approx): sum by (tenant) (sum_over_time(kv_cache_bytes_total[10m]))
- Eviction rate: increase(rate(kube_pod_container_status_terminated_reason{reason=~"OOMKilled|Evicted"}[5m]))
- Autoscaler churn: rate(keda_scaler_scale_events_total[10m])
follow_up_actions:
Action items for SRE backlog: 
- SRE-4271: Add a probe that surface per-tenant KV cache growth in >1m resolution and alert when >75% of a host's GPU memory is held by a single tenant.
- INFRA-1129: Re-evaluate autoscaler scaleDown behavior; change default min_ready_seconds to 300 and add a cooldown on scale-down when host eviction rate > 0.
- Infra PR: instrument kernel-level fragmentation metric on a subset of hosts for 2 weeks to validate hypothesis (owner: Ethan Park).
- Run a chaos experiment that simulates KV cache inflation to ensure throttling + migration order stabilizes pools within 10 minutes.
- Update oncall runbook to include the exact PromQLs and the default throttle values per tier.
retrospective_notes: What went well: quick detection via p99 alert, effective temporary throttles cleared the hotspot, team handoff was clean.\nWhat didn't go well: autoscaler defaults were too aggressive, runbook lacked clear thresholds for 'cordon and drain' vs 'throttle', missing per-tenant KV signals in dashboard.\nQuestions: should low-priority batch jobs be isolated to separate pools? what's the economic impact of adding static buffer capacity for noisy customers?
body:
Oncall log (informal, tldr + details):

Tldr: observed 3 hosts in a pool with sustained mem pressure caused by one or two tenants doing large continuous batched requests. Evictions kicked in and autoscaler reacted poorly. Quick wins were to throttle the offending tenants and migrate their long sessions off the saturated hosts; then relax autoscaler scale-down. This doc is a combination of the steps taken and a candidate runbook to formalize for future incidents.

Detailed notes:
- 03:12 UTC: p99 alert triggered for pool 'usw1-medium-gpu'. Pager overview showed elevated tail latencies across routes that use the medium model variant.
- 03:18 UTC: Checked Prometheus — top 2 tenants by tokens/sec accounted for ~72% of pool's active sessions. KV_cache_bytes_total for tenant-alpha spiked to 68% of host mem on h-usw1-gpu-05.
- 03:22 UTC: Reached out to Maya (solutions-eng) to confirm if tenant-alpha expected the large-batch; she confirmed a data processing job kicked off at 03:00 UTC.
- 03:28 UTC: We cordoned h-usw1-gpu-05 and drained opportunistically (left critical control-plane containers). Migrated two long-running sessions to fallback pool. Applied a temporary qps cap to tenant-alpha to 10qps.
- 03:35 UTC: Despite migration, two hosts still had >85% memory used; we increased pool size by +2 nodes using reserved capacity burst (available in account). Autoscaler config patched: disabled immediate scale-down.
- 03:57 UTC: p99 returned to baseline; observed reduced eviction_rate. We kept throttles for 30 minutes, then gradually lifted them while monitoring.

Notes to make the runbook less hand-wavy:
- Define exact threshold for 'cordon' (e.g., host GPU memory used > 90% AND single-tenant holding > 50%).
- Define default throttle values per customer tier (e.g., gold: 50 qps, silver: 20 qps, sandbox: 5 qps).
- Automate detection: a small service that scans per-host top tenants and emits an alert when one tenant's mem > 40% for 5m.
- Consider 'tenant-aware scheduling' to avoid co-locating multiple heavy KV tenants on same host.

Draft handoff checklist for mitigated incidents: 
1) Confirm p99 latency stable for 30 minutes.
2) Confirm eviction_count == 0 for 20 minutes.
3) Confirm no hosts remain cordoned with active workloads (list nodes and reason).
4) Create JIRA SRE- ticket with timeline + root cause + action items.
5) Assign follow-ups and schedule a 1-week post-incident sync with product for customer-facing communications.

Appendix: quick PromQLs and dashboard links we used (copy to runbook page):
- Dashboard: https://grafana.internal/d/metrics/pool-usw1
- PromQLs: see 'monitoring_queries' field in this doc.

Freeform scraps:
- We briefly considered killing the largest container on host vs migrating; migrating won because it kept customer sessions and avoided cold-starting complex models.
- Potential longer-term: dedicated 'burst' pools that accept untrusted KV growth but bill at higher rate; this could protect production pools.

Contact for follow-up: Priya Nambiar (priya@redwood.ai) and oncall rotation: #sre-oncall.
